title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
why: This asks whether the simplest intersection of linear classification rules remains efficiently learnable from ordinary examples under arbitrary distributions. A positive answer would remove a distributional assumption from a central margin-learning model; a negative answer would establish a computational obstruction even when the learner may use any efficiently evaluable representation.
status_note: The 2025 source explicitly describes the general margin-learning question as open. On 13 September 2026, a targeted small-text search and the July revisions of two 2026 abstracts did not supply a resolution of the fixed-two polynomial-time target. The 2026 proofs and their complete lower-bound parameter regimes were not independently checked; status remains source_open.
review_note: Completed individual source and formulation review on 13 September 2026; see statement_review and research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The published paper supplies the realizable two-margin-halfspace model and proves polynomial-time learning with an extra factorization assumption.
The revised preprint reports a subexponential algorithm for learning Boolean functions of a fixed number of unrestricted halfspaces; this does not yield the polynomial-time guarantee.
The revised margin-polyhedra preprint reports improved dependence on the margin and the number of halfspaces, with a dimension-dependent exponential term. Only the abstract was checked in this pass.

importance.reason: One of the simplest nonlinear concept classes whose efficient distribution-independent learnability remains unresolved.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

sentences: The intersection of two halfspaces labels a point positively when both linear inequalities hold.
This question asks whether such labels can be learned in polynomial time from independent examples under any distribution with a margin from both boundaries.
The learner may output a different kind of hypothesis, provided that predictions remain efficient.
The 2025 source proves efficient learning under an extra factorization assumption, while two 2026 preprints report broader bounds that do not by themselves meet this polynomial target.
A resolution would determine whether two linear rules can be learned efficiently without favorable structure in the example distribution.

definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.

context_blocks.text: A single separating hyperplane with a margin is a basic tractable classification model. Intersecting two such regions is already a substantial test of distribution-independent learning: allowing an arbitrary output hypothesis removes the requirement to recover two separating hyperplanes themselves.

Diakonikolas, Ma, Ren and Tzamos obtain an efficient learner when the distribution factors between the span of the two normal vectors and its orthogonal complement. Their general-model discussion on printed page 1473 leaves the distribution-free margin problem unresolved. The factorization promise is an additional assumption, not a consequence of a geometric margin.

A July 2026 revision by Alman, Patel and Servedio reports subexponential-time distribution-free learning for Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces. That running time does not meet the polynomial bound asked here.

A separate July 2026 revision by Patel and Vempala reports a margin-sensitive algorithm for intersections of a variable number of halfspaces. Its abstract does not establish a polynomial-time learner for two halfspaces; its discussion of matching lower bounds cannot be transferred to the fixed-two case without checking their parameter range.

answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified learner-existence statement or its negation in the specified arithmetic and sampling model. A positive answer includes the learner, its hypothesis representation, the polynomial training and evaluation bounds, and its distribution-independent accuracy guarantee. A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

notes: Recovered both almost-sure margin inequalities and arbitrary-distribution quantifiers from Definition 1; removed the mistaken pointer to the different question on PDF page 5.

Specified the source continuous-example problem in a uniform real-arithmetic model, with explicit sampling, confidence, improper representation and polynomial prediction costs; this is an editorial representation convention, not a claimed bit-complexity equivalence.
Added two July 2026 revisions without treating subexponential bounds or variable-number lower bounds as a resolution for two halfspaces.
